story: Hakusan is a volcano, and its summit shows it. Three peaks stand on the crest, Gozengamine (御前峰) at 2,702 metres the highest, with Kengamine and Onanjimine beside it, and between them lie eight crater lakes and dammed ponds, among them Midorigaike and Konyagaike. It last erupted in 1659. One explanation of the name is the snow: seen clearly from the coast nearby, Hakusan stays white long after the hills around it have cleared, and it is one of the highest peaks in western Japan.

The snow is the park's engine. Winter monsoon winds from the north-west bury the range, and the Ministry of the Environment reckons some 600 million tonnes of snow lie on the mountains above 500 metres. Below about 1,600 metres that water feeds some of the finest beech forest in Japan; above it come Maries' fir and Erman's birch, then creeping pine and meadows of about 250 alpine plants. More than twenty carry Hakusan in their Japanese names. Black bears, serow and golden eagles live here; rock ptarmigan, long gone, have lately been seen again.

Tradition holds that the monk Taichō (泰澄) first reached the summit in 717. By 832 three pilgrim routes, the zenjōdō (禅定道), climbed the mountain from Echizen, Kaga and Mino, starting at Heisenji Hakusan Shrine, Shirayama-hime Shrine and Nagataki Hakusan Shrine, and parts of them are still walked as trails. The inner shrine, the Okumiya, stands on the summit, and thousands of Hakusan shrines across Japan trace their worship back to this mountain. With Fuji and Tateyama it is counted among the country's three holy mountains.

Hakusan was protected as a quasi-national park in 1955 and became a national park on 12 November 1962. In 1980 UNESCO named it a biosphere reserve. Because the centre of the range is steep and roadless, it has stayed wild: the only road across the range, the Hakusan Shirakawa-go White Road, runs north of the summit, and the top is still reached only on foot. In 2023 the Hakusan Tedorigawa area, which takes in the Ishikawa side, became a UNESCO Global Geopark.
howItWorks: Hakusan is a zoned regional park, not a fenced reserve: the Ministry of the Environment sets the rules over land it does not wholly own. About 31,900 of its 49,900 hectares are national land, and the rest is public or private land. Inside the boundary are shrines, the hot springs of Chūgū and Iwama, and mountain huts at Murodō and Minami-Ryūgababa. The park takes in parts of Toyama, Ishikawa, Fukui and Gifu prefectures and seven municipalities, from Hakusan city to the village of Shirakawa.

The whole park is special zone (特別地域); there is no ordinary zone at all. More than a third of it, about 17,900 hectares, is special protection zone (特別保護地区), where picking any plant, taking a stone or lighting a fire needs a permit. In the rest, three grades of special zone control building, felling and the collecting of listed plants. For walkers this means staying on the trails and boardwalks, taking nothing and camping only at designated sites.

Other designations overlap the park. The Hakusan UNESCO Biosphere Reserve has covered it since 1980, and the Hakusan Tedorigawa UNESCO Global Geopark covers the Ishikawa side. Ishikawa Prefecture's Hakusan Nature Conservation Centre handles much of the park's day-to-day work and publishes trail, hut and road conditions. On the busiest days of the climbing season, private cars are stopped at Ichinose and a shuttle bus carries walkers the last 6 km to the trailhead at Betto-deai.

sightNotes.poi-jp-hakusan-gozengamine: Hakusan's highest summit, 2,702 metres, with the Okumiya, the inner shrine of Shirayama-hime Shrine.
sightNotes.poi-jp-hakusan-midorigaike-and-the-crate: Crater lakes north of the summit, on the Oike-meguri loop of about two hours from Murodō past the summit ponds.
sightNotes.poi-jp-hakusan-minami-ryugababa: A meadow in the saddle between Hakusan and Bessan, with boardwalks through Hakusan primroses, a hut, cabins and a campground.
sightNotes.poi-jp-hakusan-ubagataki: A broad waterfall in the Jadani gorge, seen from the Oyadani no Yu foot bath off the White Road. The path has been closed by rockfall; check before you go.
sightNotes.poi-jp-hakusan-fukube-great-waterfall: An 86-metre fall right beside the White Road, one of seven along the road on the Ishikawa side.
sightNotes.poi-jp-hakusan-shiramizu-falls: On the Gifu side, a single fall of milky-white water dropping through forest in the Ōshirakawa valley, near the start of the Hirase trail.
sightNotes.poi-jp-hakusan-itoshiro-great-cedar: A Japanese cedar thought to be about 1,800 years old, on the old Mino pilgrim route; a Special Natural Monument.

entrances: Ichinose and Betto-deai (Ishikawa), the main trailheads for the Sabō and Kankō trails to Murodō and the summit
Ōshirakawa (Gifu), start of the Hirase trail, reached from Hirase on Route 156
The Hakusan Shirakawa-go White Road, a toll road between Chūgū (Ishikawa) and Shirakawa-gō (Gifu)
Itoshiro (Gifu) for the old Mino pilgrim route, and Katsuyama (Fukui) for Mount Akausagi
planYourVisit.reservations: No entry permit is needed. The mountain huts must be booked: Hakusan Murodō, with 750 places, opens from 1 May to 15 October and serves meals from the end of June, and Nanryū Sansō at Minami-Ryūgababa from 1 July to 15 October. On peak days of the climbing season private cars may not drive between Ichinose and Betto-deai, and a shuttle bus runs instead; Ishikawa Prefecture publishes the dates each year. In 2026 the Ministry trialled advance booking of parking spaces at Betto-deai on two busy days. Check before you go.
permits: Climbing notice (登山届): required by Ishikawa Prefecture for Hakusan's active-volcano area, and by Gifu Prefecture for part of Hakusan on its side
Building, collecting plants and other regulated work in the park need permission from the Ministry of the Environment
camping: Minami-Ryūgababa Campground, in the meadow south of the summit
Ichinose has a campsite by the visitor centre
The Ōshirakawa area has a campground below the mountain; the Chūgū Onsen campsite has been closed after bear sightings, so check before you go
Tents are allowed only at designated sites
lodging: Hakusan Murodō, the large mountain hut below the summit, by reservation
Nanryū Sansō and the Minami-Ryūgababa cabins, by reservation
Hot-spring inns at Chūgū Onsen inside the park and at Shiramine below it
seasonalClosures: The Hakusan Shirakawa-go White Road closes from mid-November to early or mid-June
The huts at Murodō and Minami-Ryūgababa close in mid-October
The suspension bridge at Betto-deai has its decking removed for the winter
Ichinose Visitor Centre closes from early November to late April

chronology.text: By tradition, the monk Taichō makes the first ascent of Hakusan.
Pilgrim routes from Echizen, Kaga and Mino are opened to the summit.
The mountain is protected as Hakusan Quasi-National Park.
Hakusan becomes a national park on 12 November.
UNESCO designates the Hakusan Biosphere Reserve.
The Japan Meteorological Agency introduces eruption alert levels for Hakusan.
Hakusan Tedorigawa becomes a UNESCO Global Geopark.

safety: Hakusan is an active volcano watched by the Japan Meteorological Agency. Its eruption alert levels run from 1, 'potential for increased activity', through 2 'do not approach the crater' and 3 'do not approach the volcano' to 4 'elderly and vulnerable people evacuate' and 5 'evacuate'. Check the current level on the JMA website before you climb.

Asiatic black bears live throughout the park, and the Ministry of the Environment has issued bear warnings for it. Make noise on the trail, keep food sealed, and report any sighting at a visitor centre.
Buses to and from the trailheads are few. A day trip from Kanazawa leaves little margin, so plan around the last bus down or stay a night at Murodō.
Services close early. The huts shut in mid-October and toilets high on the mountain close for the season, so carry a portable toilet (携帯トイレ) late in the year and check the Ishikawa trail report.
regulations: On peak days private cars may not use the road between Ichinose and Betto-deai; take the shuttle bus. Motorcycles, bicycles and large coaches are not allowed on that stretch while the restriction is in force.
Camp only at designated sites, and keep to the trails and boardwalks.
The White Road is closed at night, and motorcycles are not allowed on it at any time.
Several trail toilets ask for a voluntary tip towards their upkeep; water is scarce near the summit, so use it sparingly.

weather: Hakusan has some of the deepest snow in Japan, brought by north-west winds through the winter. The huts open only from May, and Murodō serves meals only from the end of June. The climbing season, when buses run to the trailhead, is July to October; in July and August the meadows around Murodō and Minami-Ryūgababa flower, chocolate lilies among them. In autumn the beech forests of the lower slopes turn red and gold. The huts close in mid-October and the White Road in mid-November, and the mountain is left to the snow until spring.
directions: Take the Hokuriku Shinkansen to Kanazawa, about two and a half to three hours from Tokyo; on climbing-season days buses run to Ichinose from Kanazawa Station and from JR Matsutō Station via Shiramine, and a shuttle continues to Betto-deai; check with the operators before you go. Taxis also run from Komatsu Airport and Komatsu Station to the trailhead. Drivers can reach Ichinose and, except on restricted days, Betto-deai on the Hakusan Park Line road; on peak days they park at Ichinose and take the shuttle. From Gifu, Route 156 leads to Hirase and a prefectural road to Ōshirakawa. The White Road crosses from Chūgū in Ishikawa to Shirakawa-gō in Gifu.
